entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: The people who get destroyed by leverage are not unlucky. They are unprepared. They borrowed without asking: "What happens if this goes wrong? Can I survive it?" They saw only the upside — the 50% return — and were blind to the shadow. The architect does not deploy financial leverage without first calculating the worst-case scenario. Not to avoid risk — but to survive it if it comes.
entries.concern: The universal contrast between unlucky and unprepared excludes shocks and constraints beyond a borrower’s control.
entries.proposedWording: Preparation and a downside plan can reduce avoidable harm, but cannot remove every shock. Consider whether the debt remains manageable when the forecast is wrong.
entries.implementationImpact: Separate reviewed learner-source wording proposal. Retain lesson, block, prompt and response identities through explicit compiler mapping before any source release; no source change in this batch.

entries.exactPassage: The Architect's Question: You calculated the loss scenario in Part C. If that loss happened to you — if your R50,000 became significantly less — could you survive it? What is your survival plan? If you do not have one, you are not ready for leverage.
entries.concern: The falling-value calculations are Part B, while Part C is the decision.
entries.proposedWording: You calculated the loss scenario in Part B. Consider whether that outcome would be manageable and what safeguards or decision not to borrow would follow.

entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: the deposit is not just a number. It is a test. It tests your patience, your discipline, your ability to delay gratification for years. Most people fail the test. Not because they cannot save. Because they will not wait. They want the property now, so they never save for it. The people who own property are not the ones who earn the most. They are the ones who passed the test of patience.
entries.concern: The passage attributes ownership and inability to save primarily to patience, overlooking income, finance access and other constraints.
entries.proposedWording: Patience and consistency can support a deposit plan, while income, essential costs, access to finance and housing conditions also affect whether ownership is feasible.

entries.exactPassage: Question 1: Themba used 2:1 leverage on shares. When shares rose 20%, his return was 40%. When shares fell 30%, his loss was 60%. Why does leverage amplify losses more than gains in percentage terms?

entries.proposedWording: Why do these different-sized market moves produce +40% and −60% gross equity returns at 2:1? What would equal-sized upward and downward moves produce, before financing costs?
